newsitem.title: Bosnia: U.S. surveillance plane returns to Bosnian action.
newsitem.headline: U.S. surveillance plane returns to Bosnian action.

text.p: Big Brother is back watching over international peacekeepers in Bosnia.

The U.S. air force resumed using its top air-to-ground surveillance aircraft, a modified Boeing 707 first put into service in 1967 for Qantas Airways, as President Bill Clinton announced on Friday that Washington had agreed in principle to send 8,500 U.S. troops to Bosnia next year.

The $187 million aircraft, called Jake 03 of the E-8C "Joint STARS", is also back over Bosnia to review separation zones laid out in the Dayton peace pact amid concerns that a planned reduction in peacekeepers may blur tenuous borders.

The U.S. troops Clinton was referring to will join a new, smaller 31,000-man peacekeeping force expected to remain until June 1998. It will replace the current 50,000-strong force. known as IFOR, in which there are 15,000 U.S. troops.

U.S. military officials expect a pair of the planes equipped with sophisticated radar to stay in Europe for up to three months to keep tabs on the Balkans and help boost the capabilities of a reduced peacekeeping force.

"If we did not have these planes, it would take a lot more troops to have the impact on the ground that we can provide," said Colonel Ben Robinson, who heads the 93rd Air Control Wing based at Robins air base in Georgia.
"Our mission is provide information," he said of the first of the new series of missions over Bosnia. "And we give ground commanders an unparalleled edge to enforce the peace treaty."

The planes, designed by Northrop Grumman in the 1980s for war against the Soviets, will fly mostly at night to cover the withdrawal of the army's First Armored Division that joined the international peacekeeping force last December.

The old Boeing planes, which can fly for up to 21 hours with the aid of inflight refuelling, will also watch over the new U.S. troops Clinton said were to join the smaller, follow-on international force and their redeployment in the region.
"We are going back to a period of movement in Bosnia after creating a static place," said Robinson, a 49-year-old former B-52 bomber pilot who also flew army helicopters in Vietnam.
"And we are here to keep it fair, especially at night when groups are most apt to want to move around," said Robinson.

The planes first flew over Bosnia last December as U.S. troops joined the controversial peacekeeping force, flying 95 missions as American forces built bridges over the Sava River and then fanned out in Bosnia to separate warring factions.
Real-time images from the plane have allowed U.S. ground commanders to help keep track of problem areas, particularly mass grave sites, without having troops on site.

"The radar was powerful enough that we have picked out vehicles approaching grave sites and given ample warning to troops on the ground to intercept them," said Technical Sergeant Brian Lewis of Arlington, Virginia, on the flight.

Inside the darkened cabin of the aircraft, which criss-crosses some 29,000 feet (8,800 metres) above the former war zone in 15-mile (24 km) sweeps, rows of operators sit at computer workstations monitoring colour data from the 27-foot (8.2 metre) radar system on the belly of the aircraft.

Yellow and magenta dots on the screen represent moving vehicles laid over computerised maps of Bosnia. A trio of snaking yellow lines marks the borders to separate factions, helping to detect any forces moving out of their zones.

Initial lines of coloured dots can be transformed into photographic-like images and video that can be sent around the world with detail so sharp that the difference between the height of trees can be distinguished.
"We could be up here and see a group cross a border and send live pictures to United Nations," Robinson said. "That would attract some attention."
Prototypes of the aircraft now flying over Bosnia were first put into service during the Gulf War. Northrop is contracted to deliver 19 of the planes, which have a 21-member crew.
But the plane has its limits -- it cannot see through the vast range of mountains in the Bosnian landscape, blocking some areas, including Sarajevo, from being quickly examined.
"Looking at Bosnia on some of the radar pictures looks like someone took some tin foil and crinkled it up," said one crew member aboard the flight. "The ground terrain is difficult."
